sources.title: Wen-Wei Lin, Lecture Notes of Matrix Computations
sources.locator: Complete 339-page lecture notes inspected. §3.2.2, PDF pp. 65–66: Algorithm 3.2.6 for Householder bidiagonalization, exact upper bidiagonal reduction, and SVD composition. §6.3, PDF pp. 229–231: implicit shifted QR on B*B, Givens bulge chase, implicit-Q relation, and the zero-diagonal split. §6.3, PDF p. 238: singular-value absolute perturbation corollary. §3.2.1, PDF pp. 53–55: rank-deficient least squares, pseudoinverse composition, and the Kahan CPQR warning.

contents.name: Algorithm 3.2.6: finite Householder steps reduce a tall matrix to upper bidiagonal form with accumulated orthogonal factors
§3.2.2: exact bidiagonal reduction is a left/right unitary equivalence and composes with the bidiagonal SVD
§6.3: shifted QR of B*B can be applied directly to B by alternating Givens rotations and chasing one bulge
§6.3: the final bidiagonal block is a unitary left/right transform of the prior block; zero offdiagonal couplings split the problem
Corollary 6.3.2: each ordered singular value changes by at most the spectral norm of an additive perturbation
§3.2.1 Algorithm 3.2.5: compose a rank-revealing factorization with the canonical pseudoinverse for rank-deficient least squares
§3.2.1: ordinary greedy CPQR can fail to detect near rank deficiency; the source's Kahan matrix is not the local 4-by-4 witness used here
The notes defer the full bidiagonal QR convergence proof; this page makes no convergence-rate claim for its finite-budget procedure
contents.reason: The source explicitly defers the convergence discussion to a later chapter; the local algorithm returns an inconclusive status at its sweep cap and proves no unconditional convergence rate.

sources.title: Ming Gu and Stanley C. Eisenstat, Efficient Algorithms for Computing a Strong Rank-Revealing QR Factorization, SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 17(4) (1996), 848–869
sources.locator: Complete 22-page paper inspected. §2, PDF pp. 3–4: greedy QR with column pivoting and Example 1 showing it can fail a polynomial strong bound. §3, PDF pp. 5–6: Lemma 3.1's exact swap-volume ratio and Theorem 3.2's block singular-value comparisons. §4, PDF pp. 7–8: practical strong RRQR swap criterion and finite termination argument.

contents.name: §2 Example 1: classical greedy CPQR need not produce a strong rank-revealing factorization
Lemma 3.1: interchanging selected and trailing columns changes selected volume by sqrt(|X_ij|^2+(gamma_j(C) omega_i(A))^2)
Theorem 3.2: the combined stopping score yields the factor sqrt(1+f^2 k(n-k)) in both block singular comparisons
Algorithms 3–5: swaps are selected by coefficient and residual terms, and strict volume increase gives finite termination
§5 floating-point operation count and detailed implementation updates for the published algorithm
contents.reason: This page proves exact-arithmetic existence, termination and singular-value comparisons; it does not claim the paper's complexity or floating-point stability analysis for the locally specified procedure.

sources.title: James Demmel and W. Kahan, Accurate Singular Values of Bidiagonal Matrices, LAPACK Working Note 3 (1990)
sources.locator: Complete 42-page working note fetched; the complete relevant §2 perturbation argument was inspected (PDF pp. 3–10), including Theorem 2, Corollary 2 and their proofs. §3, PDF pp. 11–12, contrasts conventional shifted QR's absolute-error behavior with the stronger zero-shift relative-accuracy algorithm.

contents.name: §2 Corollary 2: componentwise relative changes in bidiagonal entries perturb every positive singular value relatively, independent of magnitude
Theorem 3: arbitrary additive matrix perturbations give an absolute singular-value error bound
§1 and §3: conventional bidiagonal QR may lose relative accuracy for tiny singular values; the paper's zero-shift algorithm supplies stronger guarantees under a different backward-error analysis
§3–§8 implementation and full forward-stability proof for the paper's special zero-shift algorithm
contents.reason: The present page does not implement or claim the special zero-shift algorithm's componentwise backward stability; its relative theorem is explicitly conditional on a stronger componentwise-relative perturbation input.
